div.p: line 1 (of Affiliation): dept. name of organization line 2-name of organization, acronyms acceptable line 3-City, Authors Name/s per 2nd Affiliation (Author) line 1 (of Affiliation): dept. name of organization line 2-name of organization, acronyms acceptable line 3-City, Country Abstract-With the interesting of researchers to develop the scheduling of multiprocessor and distributed system in hard real time embedded systems, we present a new locking protocol called Minimizing multiple-Priority Inversion Protocol (MPIP), in this protocol, we proposed a novel mechanism to turn from preemptive to non-preemptive state to minimize multiple-priority inversion caused by low priority task on local processor. We focus on distributed locking semaphore and we showed its ability to lock the shared memory, thus; working in Multi-processor environment. We assumed all shared resources as global to avoid resource nested. With properties of our protocol, we define a new upper bound blocking time. We submit our proposal to experimental evaluation to compare it with MPCP protocol in term of hard real time schedulability.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: Toward improving the scheduling for multiprocessor hard real time system, there has been much recent interest in techniques for scheduling real-time workloads on multiprocessors an increasing effort is being dedicated in the real-time literature for multiprocessor scheduling, analysis and design methodologies. Particularly, one of the key challenges in this context is constituted by resource synchronization protocols [19]. For the resource synchronization, there are two classic locking protocols: the multiprocessor priority ceiling protocol (M-PCP) [14] and the distributed priority ceiling protocol (D-PCP) [2]. While these protocols are probably the most widely known (and taught) locking protocols for multiprocessor real-time applications, they were developed at a time (over 20 years ago) when such applications were deemed to be mostly of academic interest only. With the advent of multicore technologies, this is clearly no longer the case. And toward to treat several shortcomings of previouslyproposed real-time multiprocessor locking schemes [5], a flexible real-time locking protocols for multiprocessors FMLP was presented [5].
And Multi-Processor Stack-Based Scheduling Protocol MSRP [4] was developed.

Motivated by this, we discussed in this paper how to give a precise equation to the upper bound blocking time, presenting a novel idea to minimize multiple-priority inversion by changing the behavior of task from preemptive to nonpreemptive with a new mechanism. We presented a new locking protocol called MPIP.

Two main approaches for scheduling real-time systems on multiprocessors exist; global and partitioned scheduling. Under global scheduling, e.g., Global Earliest Deadline First (G-EDF), tasks scheduled by a single scheduler and each task can be executed on any processor. A single global queue used for storing jobs. A job can be preempted on a processor and resumed on another processor, i.e., migration of tasks among processors permitted. Under a partitioned scheduling, tasks statically assigned to processors and then within each processor scheduled by a uniprocessor scheduling protocol, e.g., Rate Monotonic (RM) and EDF. Each processor associated with a separate ready queue for scheduling task jobs.

In this paper, our proposal did under partitioned scheduling for distributed semaphore because partitioned scheduling protocols have been used more often and supported (with fixed priority scheduling) widely by commercial real-time operating systems [18] [20].

Contribution. We present a new multiprocessor synchronization, called Minimizing multiple-Priority Inversion Protocol (MPIP), the protocol derived from DPCP and MPCP classical protocols with keeping the property of DPCP in it, using in distributed system. This new protocol has three characteristics. First, minimize the multiple-priority inversion. Second, avoid nested resource accesses in common case. Third, reduce the upper bound blocking time, thus reduce the worst case response time (WCRT).

Organization. In II we reviewed the related work. In III introduced background and notation of system model. In IV described our protocol' design. In V presented the upper bound blocking time and response time analysis. Whereas in VI, we conducted schedulability experiments and the results. Finally, we concluded this paper in VII.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: With working on multiprocessor synchronization, Rajkumar et al. [2] proposed the first suspension-based protocol distributed priority-ceiling protocol (DPCP), where the jobs do not access remote global resources directly. The DPCP, suitable to use in distributed systems where processor can't share memory. Multi-processor ceiling protocol (MPCP) is direct extension of the well-known Priority Ceiling Protocol (PCP) [3,14]. MPCP relies on shared memory to support global resources, but with problem of multiple-priority Furkan Rabee1,2 , Yong Liao 1 , Maolin Yang 1 inversion on local processor when the low priority jobs held the shared resources, and the second problem is the nested on local shared resource. In later work, Gai et al. [5] proposed a spin-based protocol, the Multiprocessor Stack Resource Protocol (MSRP), which works on both P-FP and partitioned Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling systems, its realized via spinning (i.e., busy-waiting). Block et al. presented the Flexible Multiprocessor Locking Protocol (FMLP) [5], which differentiates long and short critical sections, blocking enforced by suspension for long critical sections, and spinning for short critical sections. Recently, Easwaran et al. [6] presented a suspension-based protocol for global scheduling systems. Brandenburg et al. [1,7] discussed priority inversion in blocking time analysis and presented the OMLP class of protocols. In other work aimed at protecting temporal behavior of tasks in open real-time systems, Faggioli et al. [8] presented the Multiprocessor Bandwidth Inheritance protocol (MBWI). Empirical studies [9,10] indicate that the MPCP is more efficient than the spin-based MSRP by its nature of suspension and priority boosting, especially when critical sections are long. Besides, the MPCP may behave better if the schedulability analysis is less pessimistic [12].

In order to provide upper bounds on the blocking time and worst case response time for tasks on multiprocessors, Lakshmanan et al. [11] consider the deferrable task model in [13], the key idea is to bound the response time of each critical section within a job and sum them together.

div.head: A. Task Model
div.p: A set of n periodic tasks T = {T 1 , T 2 , …, T n } are scheduled on multi-processor, besides the m processor P 1 , P 2 , …, P m .

Tasks in T are indexed by decreasing order of priorities, so i < j represents that the priority of T i is higher than that of T j . A periodic task potentially generates n jobs; each job has the same priority as that assigned to the task. The l th job of T i is denoted as J i,l , an arbitrary job of T i is also denoted as J i,* . J i,l is raised at r i,l and finishes at f i,l , it is said to be pending during [r i,l , f i,l ]. The WCRT of T i is defined as R i = l max(f i,l -r i,l ).

div.head: B. Allocation Algorithem
div.p: In this paper we used Rate Monotonic Best Fit (RMBF), which defined as follows: allocates the task to the processor with smallest available utilization, on which it can be feasibly scheduled. RMBF orders tasks increasingly according to their periods, before the allocation process. Tasks can be feasibly scheduled according to the schedulability condition IP [16].

div.head: Schedulability condition IP (Increasing Period).
div.p: In condition IP [23], it is required that the periods of the tasks are ordered increasingly, thus the timing constraints of the task set must be known a priori. Condition IP, introduced by Dhall and Liu [23] is used in the implementation of the multiprocessor algorithms Rate Monotonic Next Fit, Rate Monotonic First Fit, and Rate Monotonic Best Fit.

div.head: C. Real Time Semaphore
div.p: Tasks may share serially reusable resources (such as coprocessors, I/O ports, or shared data structures, etc.). Access to shared resources is governed by a locking protocol that ensures mutual exclusion. There are two major types of semaphore protocols. In shared-memory locking protocols, tasks execute critical sections locally, in the sense that each task accesses shared resources directly from the processor on which it is scheduled. For example, this is the case under the classic Multiprocessor Priority-Ceiling Protocol (MPCP) [3,14]. In contrast, in distributed locking protocols, each resource is accessed only from a designated synchronization processor (or cluster 1 ). Such protocols, which derive their name from the fact that they could also be used in distributed systems (i.e., in the absence of shared memory), this is the case under another classic Distributed Priority-Ceiling Protocol (DPCP) [2].
In this paper, we focus on distributed real-time semaphore protocol and the ability to lock the shared memory on the same time by requesting the shared resources using Remote Procedure Calls (RPCs).

div.head: IV. PROTOCOL DESIGN
div.p: In this paper, we proposed for each shared resource would generate one RPC , that is mean each shared resource will be served with two stubs, server stub at the site of shared resource and client stub at the site of tasks, executed the critical section on a pseudo-processor, figure 1 illustrates our proposal.

We proposed the pseudo-processor to execute the critical section where the local area network LAN will manage the requesting to the shared resources with generating server/client communication by using local host IP: 127.0.0.1. While each server/client stubs will call isolated semaphore. The local area network will be responsible for managing the RPC. Since by using local host IP, our protocol can work on multiprocessor system, and can share memory too. The cause of using RPC, that to keep the generality of the protocol to be still has the ability to work on distributed system, where by user selection, can be specify the function of the protocol.

div.head: B. Minimizing the Multiple-Priority Inversion Protocol
div.p: In this section, we described our protocol's synchronization rules. First, we described the execution control policy which we used, and secondly, we described the synchronization rules.

div.head: 1) Execution control policies :
div.p: An execution control policy (ECP) is defined as a mechanism to compensate for the scheduling penalties incurred by tasks due to remote blocking [11] and the two main policies are: a) Suspend: The task is suspended during remote blocking, enabling lower priority tasks to execute.
b) Spin: The task continues to spin on the remote critical section, preventing lower priority tasks from executing. In this paper we focus on "Suspend" execution control policy.

div.head: 2) Protocol synchronization rules:
div.p: In this part we described our protocol rules, where we presented innovative idea to minimize the multiple-priority inversion caused by low priority jobs to the higher priority jobs when they try to hold the shared resource on local processor. We used figure 2 to illustrate these rules; which are as follows:

P1. If the lower priority task is requested to any shared resource and it is blocked by other remote agents (jobs), the agent of lower priority task can preempt the higher priority task for one time to any shared resource, and then the higher priority task will be non-preempted, this is for each job for one task. div.head: 3) protocol's properties
div.p: We represented the properties of our protocol as follows:
Lemma 1 No nested occur in common case.

Proof. According to the R1 and R2 we treated with all shared resources as global, thus; there is no nested occur, over that we depend on the same properties of DPCP and MPCP, which disallow nested occur (for global resources).

Lemma 2 This protocol is deadlock-free. Proof: Deadlock can occur if there exists a circular chain of jobs where each job in the chain is blocked on a resource, requested by the next job in the chain, this is not permitted because:

x The lower priority job has only one time to preempt the higher priority task. x Jobs which acquire shared resource are priority boosted, thus, the higher priority job can preempt the lower priority directly after the lower priority task give up the shared resource.

div.head: 1) Experiemental setup
div.p: Our experiments evaluate the ration of schedulable task sets on 8-processor(system) with different characteristics. We described factors that affect the schedulability as follows: x The total system utilization U i which represents the work load of the system (vary from 0.8 to 8 step 0.8).

x The critical section length, which affects the shared resource usage is represents as percentage from the WCET, which start from 5 % to 25% , step 1%. x The number of shared resources for whole system is ten.

An experiment scenario consists of the above parameters. The results of our experiment show a total of 94 scenarios. We select a system utilization cap (in (0, 8]) in each scenario, based on which we generate tasks as follows. Task periods are generated from [50ms, 1000ms] with uniform distribution; [0.01, 0.36] for light-loaded tasks, with those utilization types we tested the ratio of schedulable task set.

Priorities are assigned to tasks according to the Rate Monotonic (RM) algorithm [21]. The WCET of each task T i is determined by the selected period and utilization. Utilization exceeds the selected system utilization cap, in that case the last generated task is discarded. If the remaining utilization gap is within the range of values allowed for the task utilization, we generate a task that exactly fit the utilization gap and add it to the task set; otherwise, we regenerate the task set. A total number of 3050 task sets are generated for each scenario, and are tested using different schedulability algorithms.

div.head: 1) Result and discussion
div.p: In this section we compare the performance of our proposal with MPCP performance. The proposed method outperforms and other method in all of the scenarios shown in figure 4 to 6. Each processor contains more than one task, since the platform consist of 8 processors. If processor contains two tasks, two shared resource and each shared resource acquired by one critical section, that is mean one request per shared resource, the total requests are 8× 2 = 16 request, while the number of lockers are equal to than 16.

Figure 4 shows the ratio of schedulable task sets with two critical sections per task. The critical section length is 5% of WCET, the maximum numbers of shared resource are two. With increasing the total system utilization caused reduce the schedule task sets. Since the performances of the two methods close to each other when the total system utilization is less than 4, we evaluate each method by varying the other factors at that point.

Figure 5 show the performance of the methods where the scheduled task sets decreased with increasing the length of critical section because increasing the blocking time and this effect on the performance of response time for the tasks. The total system utilization is 4, number of critical sections per task are 2, maximum numbers of shared resources are two.

Figure 6 show the performance of each method with increasing the number of shared resource where the total system utilization is 4, the critical section length is 5% from WCET, the numbers of critical sections per task are 10.

div.head: VII. CANCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: In this paper, we present (Minimizing multiple-Priority Inversion Protocol), which capable of being implemented on system scheduled by partitioned scheduling for distributed locking semaphore, and this is first protocol shows the ability of distributed semaphore to lock the shared memory with keeping of generality for using in distributed system by the exploitation of the local area network (LAN) to manage the shared resource. Deemed all shared resources as global that give an advantage which prevents the resource nested. On the other hand , this protocol minimized the problem of multi priority inversion where MPCP and DPCP protocols suffer from it, by give a novel mechanism for changing from preemptive to non-preemptive suspension control policy without depending on busy-wait in spin policy. From the rules of our protocol we derived precise equations for upper bound blocking time and it is represented by equation 4 to equation 9. We tested our proposal and it was outperform on MPCP protocol. For future direction, we will suggest the researchers to try to implement this protocol by design a real time software" linux micro operating system", and test the performance of this protocol with other locking protocols.
